metadata.title: When Change Just Produces a Different Kind of Wrong
metadata.topic: Detecting whether a change to an agentic/prompting system genuinely helped or just relocated the failure mode
metadata.purpose: Teach the epistemics of change in AI systems: a fix reshapes the error surface, it doesn't erase it. Paired-not-aggregate, severity-weighted, judge-audited, cause-not-symptom, append-to-the-ledger.
metadata.source: Bear's research prompt — How to Tell When a Change Helps vs. Just Produces a Different Kind of Wrong
metadata.notes: Kokoro am_onyx, free (IN-FOR-BEAR LAW). GATE P before any Kokoro (VOICE-LOCK) swap. Deep-explainer: 7 acts, 33 body beats, VOX 21% / MANIM 27% / REMOTION 42% / CARD 9%. Vox runs R0 (B07-B08) and R1 (B28-B30). Never publish.

beats.narration_text: Hey — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's what I typed into Claude: I changed a prompt to fix a bug, and it stopped. So did I fix it — or did I just move it somewhere I'm not looking? Turns out that question has a real answer.

props.topic: Detecting whether a change to an agentic/prompting system genuinely helped or just relocated the failure mode
props.segment: When Change Just Produces a Different Kind…
props.command: When Change Just Produces a Different Kind of Wrong?
I changed a prompt to stop my agent hallucinating tool calls. How do I know the change actually helped — and didn't just trade that failure for a worse one I'm not testing for?
output: Every change reshapes the error surface — it doesn't erase it.

beats.narration_text: Every system that can fail has an error surface — the whole set of ways it goes wrong. Change a prompt, a tool schema, a retrieval step, and you're not sliding from wrong to right on a dial. You're reshaping that surface.

props.title: When Change Just Produces a Different Kind of Wrong

production_viz.label: error surface
production_viz.mechanic: A 3D-ish heightmap terrain of failure; as a change lands, one peak flattens and a new one rises elsewhere — reshaped, not removed.

beats.narration_text: Press one failure mode down and a different one routinely bulges up somewhere else. The trouble: most iteration loops check exactly one thing — did the bug I was staring at stop happening.
beats.new_visual_element: Surface cross-section: one bump pressed, neighbor rises

production_viz.label: push-down / pop-up
production_viz.mechanic: 2D cross-section of the surface; a finger presses one bump down and the adjacent bump rises by the same area. Labels: 'fixed' / 'new'.

beats.narration_text: Economists named this — Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Optimize the symptom you can see, and you quietly degrade the thing you can't.
beats.prompt: pantry/B03-goodhart.png — archival portrait of economist Charles Goodhart. Tier 3: archival photo first; the photograph's rights govern. Vox-treated: desat ~80%, Claude cream stage, grain, terracotta underline on 'a measure becomes a target'.

production_viz.label: Goodhart's Law
production_viz.mechanic: Ken Burns push toward the face; terracotta hand-drawn underline draws on under the key clause.

beats.narration_text: It's Goodhart's Law wearing a hoodie — and it's an ordinary regression bug: the fix that closes one ticket and silently opens another. One difference: a compiler fails the same way every time. A model's failure space is open-ended, stochastic, and only shows under the right inputs.

production_viz.label: deterministic vs stochastic
production_viz.mechanic: Split screen: left, identical input → identical output repeated (clean); right, identical input → a scatter of outputs. Divergence pattern.

beats.narration_text: So before you touch anything, you write down what 'helped' would even mean — because you cannot detect a shift you never specified.
beats.new_visual_element: Pipeline: define → measure → compare → judge → ledger

production_viz.label: the loop
production_viz.mechanic: Five-node flow lights its first node: define → measure → compare → judge → ledger. Reused as a recurring spine across acts.

beats.narration_text: Start with an error taxonomy — the named ways this system fails. Not 'wrong answers.' Categories: hallucinated tool call, premature stop, over-verification loop, ignored constraint, format drift, right answer for the wrong reason, silent scope creep.
beats.new_visual_element: Isotype grid of labeled failure categories

production_viz.label: error taxonomy
production_viz.mechanic: Seven labeled isotype cells populate one by one, each with a small glyph: hallucinated tool call, premature stop, over-verification loop, ignored constraint, format drift, right-answer/wrong-reason, silent scope creep.

beats.narration_text: Then a held-out eval set — thirty to a hundred cases, stratified across those categories. Here's the trap: if your set is only the cases you already know are broken, you'll only ever see improvement. Never regression.
beats.prompt: pantry/B07-specimen.png (Tier 1) — a card-catalog / specimen index tray; wide, high-res so the tight 1.9x hold is sharp. Same plate as B08 (this is run R0). Terracotta ring on the single focused card.

production_viz.label: held-out set (detail)
production_viz.mechanic: Ken Burns tight on ONE index card; ring highlights it. Handoff to B08's pull-back.

beats.narration_text: Score per category, not one pass-fail: did each case fail the same way, a new way, or not at all? Store it as a versioned file next to the prompt — so eval drift shows up in a diff, same as prompt drift.
beats.new_visual_element: Pull back to the whole stratified tray
beats.prompt: pantry/B07-specimen.png (same plate as B07) — camera pulls back from the one card to the whole stratified tray, cases grouped by category. Last beat of run R0 (no handoff).

production_viz.label: held-out set (whole)
production_viz.mechanic: Continuous pull-back from B07's card to the full tray; category groupings become visible.

beats.narration_text: And the discipline that makes it all work: for every fix, before you run it, write down what you think it might break. That one field makes you look for the thing you predicted — not just the thing you hoped for.
beats.new_visual_element: YAML case card, regression_risk line lit

production_viz.label: regression_risk
production_viz.mechanic: A small eval-case YAML card types out; the `regression_risk:` line highlights terracotta. Fields: id, category, expected_behavior, known_failure_mode, regression_risk.

beats.act: ACT III — One Draw Is Noise
beats.narration_text: Now the part everyone skips. Model outputs are sampled, not fixed — even at temperature zero, with tools and multi-turn state, the variance is real. One before-and-after on one example tells you almost nothing. It could be luck.

production_viz.label: sampled, not fixed
production_viz.mechanic: A single input token fires repeatedly into a spreading scatter of different outputs; a lone 'before/after' pair is highlighted then swamped by the spread.

beats.act: ACT III — One Draw Is Noise
beats.narration_text: So run each case five to ten times, before and after. Compare distributions — not single draws.
beats.new_visual_element: Two pass-rate distributions, before vs after

production_viz.label: distributions
production_viz.mechanic: Two overlaid histograms of per-case pass rate (before / after) build up from repeated trials.

beats.act: ACT III — One Draw Is Noise
beats.narration_text: And compare them paired — same case, before versus after — not as averages. A system that fixes twenty cases and breaks fifteen different ones shows the same net plus-five as one that fixes twenty and breaks nothing. Same headline. Opposite reality.
beats.new_visual_element: Two rivers both netting +5, one churning with cross-flow

production_viz.label: paired, not net
production_viz.mechanic: Two Sankey-ish flows both ending at net +5: the top flows straight (20 up, 0 down); the bottom churns (20 up-crossings AND 15 down-crossings). Same endpoint, visibly different traffic.

beats.act: ACT III — One Draw Is Noise
beats.narration_text: The honest tool has a name — McNemar's test — built for exactly this: paired yes/no outcomes on the same items. It looks only at the cases that flipped. And when few flip, it tells you the truth you don't want: not enough evidence yet.

production_viz.label: McNemar 2x2
production_viz.mechanic: A 2x2 table (before pass/fail x after pass/fail); the two off-diagonal 'discordant' cells highlight; the concordant cells dim. A small 'n discordant is small → low power' note.

beats.act: ACT III — One Draw Is Noise
beats.narration_text: The cases that flipped pass-to-fail? That's not noise to wave off. That's your different kind of wrong, showing up on camera. Investigate those before you ship — not the aggregate that's smiling at you.
beats.new_visual_element: Results list; newly_failing rows pulled out and ringed

production_viz.label: newly_failing
production_viz.mechanic: A per-case results list; the rows that went pass→fail lift out and ring terracotta; a big green aggregate '+8%' sits above, ignored.

beats.narration_text: A pass rate climbing seventy to seventy-eight tells you nothing alone. Watch: format drift falls twelve percent to two — good. But hallucinated tool calls climb ten to eighteen. Net score up. And you just traded a cosmetic typo for a call that can delete data.

production_viz.label: the trade
production_viz.mechanic: Two category bars animate before→after: format_drift 12→2 (shrinks), hallucinated_tool_call 10→18 (grows). Bars sized by magnitude; the growing one flashes 'can delete data'.

beats.narration_text: That's the crux. Aggregate metrics are severity-blind — a formatting nit and a destructive tool call count the same. So weight each category by cost-of-failure and track the weighted error surface, not the raw count.

production_viz.label: weight by cost
production_viz.mechanic: Equal-count bars re-scale as a severity weight multiplies each; the 'destructive' category balloons, the 'cosmetic' one shrinks; a weighted total redraws — nonlinear-severity idea, no invented formula shown.

beats.narration_text: One catch: the thing labeling which category a failure belongs to is often another model — a judge. And a judge is a prompted system with its own error surface. Which is the next problem.
beats.new_visual_element: Judge-model box with a small warning ring (bridge to Act V)

production_viz.label: the judge appears
production_viz.mechanic: A 'judge model' box slides in to stamp category labels; a small terracotta warning ring pulses on it — hands off visually to Act V.

beats.act: ACT V — The Judge Is a System Too
beats.narration_text: Iterate against the same eval set over and over and two things rot quietly. First, the prompt overfits — it learns your fifty cases' exact wording instead of the underlying failure. Gains that don't generalize.
beats.sparkline: The Judge Is a System Too
beats.prompt: pantry/B19-panel.png (Tier 1–2) — a panel/bench of judges, or a row of adjudicators. Vox-treated; serif spark line 'The Judge Is a System Too'.

production_viz.label: the judge
production_viz.mechanic: Ken Burns across a bench/panel; slow push.

beats.act: ACT V — The Judge Is a System Too
beats.narration_text: Second, the judge overfits. If a model grades your outputs and you tune to please it, you optimize for what it likes — length, hedging, authoritative-sounding phrasing — instead of the task actually getting done.
beats.new_visual_element: Two diverging paths: task-success vs judge-pleasing

production_viz.label: pleasing the judge
production_viz.mechanic: A path forks: 'task success' (narrow, honest) vs 'judge-pleasing' (wide, decorated — length/hedge/authority icons). Tuning drifts toward the wrong branch.

beats.act: ACT V — The Judge Is a System Too
beats.narration_text: And these biases are documented, not folklore. Position bias: the order you list candidates changes the winner. Verbosity bias. Authority bias, and sycophancy — a polite hedge can swing a grader all by itself.

production_viz.label: documented biases
production_viz.mechanic: Chips light one by one: position/order, verbosity, apology, authority-phrasing. On 'position', two candidates swap order and the winner flips.

beats.act: ACT V — The Judge Is a System Too
beats.narration_text: So you build guards: a frozen canary set you never look at until the end; paraphrased inputs, so a fix has to generalize to count; randomized candidate order; and a panel of judges, not one — a panel cancels a single model's blind spot.

production_viz.label: the guards
production_viz.mechanic: Four guards assemble: a locked 'canary' vault, a paraphrase transform on an input, an order-shuffler, and a panel of N judges voting (single judge's blind spot greyed out).

beats.act: ACT V — The Judge Is a System Too
beats.narration_text: And track why a case now passes. If it's a narrow keyword patch that happens to satisfy the grader, flag it — narrow-fix debt — even when it currently scores green.
beats.new_visual_element: A passing case tagged narrow-fix debt

production_viz.label: narrow-fix debt
production_viz.mechanic: A green 'PASS' case flips over to reveal a narrow keyword-match underneath; a terracotta 'narrow-fix debt' tag stamps on despite the green.

beats.narration_text: Here's the one that gets everybody. An agent gives a hedgy, unhelpful answer and you want it to stop. But that one symptom has at least three causes: retrieval returned weak evidence and it correctly hedged; the prompt over-rewards caution; or it never looked at the evidence it had and hedged on reflex.

production_viz.label: one symptom, three causes
production_viz.mechanic: A single 'hedgy answer' node branches into three causes: weak-evidence (correct hedge), over-cautious prompt, didn't-look reflex.

beats.narration_text: So you write 'don't hedge, be confident.' It suppresses the symptom for all three. But it's only right for cause two. For one and three you just built a new failure — confident, wrong answers — which are worse than a hedgy answer pointing the right way.
beats.new_visual_element: One fix on all three branches; two turn red confident-wrong

production_viz.label: the misfire
production_viz.mechanic: The 'be confident' fix drops onto all three branches; branch 2 turns green (correct), branches 1 and 3 turn red and relabel 'confident + wrong'.

beats.narration_text: That's the most common different-kind-of-wrong in agent tuning: trading calibrated uncertainty for false confidence, because false confidence scores better on a lazy rubric. The fix is cheap — write a one-line causal hypothesis before you change anything.

production_viz.label: calibrated → false confidence
production_viz.mechanic: A calibration dial swings from 'calibrated' to 'false confidence'; a terracotta warning zone at the far end; a small 'causal hypothesis:' field types in as the cheap guard.

beats.narration_text: The last move is stolen straight from software, because it's the same problem. Every bug you fix becomes a permanent test case. Added to the suite. Never removed.
beats.new_visual_element: Archival regression log / punch-card, tight on one record
beats.prompt: pantry/B28-ledger.png (Tier 1–2) — a wide, high-res archival software-testing artifact: a regression log, punch-card stack, or bug ledger. Same plate across R1 (B28/B29/B30), must survive the 2.0x zoom. Spark 'The Ledger'.

production_viz.label: one record
production_viz.mechanic: Ken Burns tight (2.0x) on a single logged test record; handoff to B29 pull-back.

beats.narration_text: So a case that flips from failing to passing — then quietly regresses six versions later — gets caught, because the case is still there, still running.
beats.new_visual_element: Pull back to the whole append-only ledger
beats.prompt: pantry/B28-ledger.png (same plate) — pull back from the one record to the full append-only ledger; rows stack, none deleted. Middle beat of R1.

production_viz.label: the whole ledger
production_viz.mechanic: Continuous pull-back to the full ledger; a terracotta 'regressed' marker blinks on a row that had gone green.

beats.narration_text: Version the suite alongside the prompt and you can bisect a regression the way git bisect finds the bad commit — narrow it to the two versions it appeared between.
beats.new_visual_element: Pan along a version history; two adjacent versions ring terracotta
beats.prompt: pantry/B28-ledger.png (same plate) — pan right to a version timeline; bisect narrows to two adjacent versions, ringed terracotta. Last beat of R1 (no handoff).

production_viz.label: bisect
production_viz.mechanic: Pan to a version rail; a bisect halves the range twice and lands on two adjacent versions, ringed.

beats.narration_text: And none of this is vibes derived from first principles. Behavioral testing — CheckList. Static benchmarks getting overfit — Dynabench. Multi-metric reporting so trade-offs stay visible — HELM. Panels of judges — PoLL. The pattern has receipts.

production_viz.label: the receipts
production_viz.mechanic: Four citation chips drop in with their one-line point: CheckList (behavioral), Dynabench (overfit), HELM (multi-metric), PoLL (panel). Each re-verified at Gate F.

beats.narration_text: One last check, before you even run the comparison: ask whether a prompt edit is the right lever at all. Sometimes the honest fix is a different model, a guardrail, or a system-design change — not one more instruction bolted on.
beats.new_visual_element: Lever menu — prompt / model / guardrail / design

production_viz.label: the right lever
production_viz.mechanic: Four levers — prompt / model / guardrail / system-design; the hand reaches past 'prompt' (not auto-selected) to weigh the others.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A change reshapes the error surface — it doesn't erase it. Name your failure taxonomy and a stratified held-out set before you touch the prompt. Compare paired runs, not aggregate scores. Weight failures by severity. Remember the judge is a system too. Fix the cause, not the symptom. And keep an append-only ledger — so a change that helps can't quietly stop helping.

artifactLines: A change reshapes the error surface — it doesn't erase it.
Name the taxonomy and a stratified held-out set first.
Compare paired runs, not aggregate scores.
Weight failures by severity; watch the shape.
The judge is a system too — canary, paraphrase, panel.
Fix the cause, not the symptom.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's one to run on your own work. Paste this into Claude: I changed a prompt in my agent to fix one failure mode, and I have before-and-after results on a held-out eval set — per case, with failure categories. Walk me through, in order: one, the paired diff — which cases flipped pass-to-fail, not just the net pass rate; two, whether any newly-failing case is a new or higher-severity category than the one I fixed; and three, which of my newly-passing cases might be narrow pattern-matches that wouldn't survive a paraphrase. Be skeptical by default. That third question is the one that'll surprise you — run it and count how many of your wins don't survive a reworded input.

Be skeptical by default.
